image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #704: Principle of Explosion

titleText.es: ¿Quiere que lleve cucuruchos de galleta? Ah, claro, para el vino. Un segundo, déjeme derivar el número de tarjeta de crédito de su hijo y me pondré en camino.
titleText.en: You want me to pick up waffle cones? Oh, right, for the wine. One sec, let me just derive your son's credit card number and I'll be on my way.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #704, published 2010-02-19; their title texts are preserved exactly. The Spanish archive credits Gabriel Rodríguez Alberich as translator. The authored transcript follows the visible Spanish raster: it joins the printed line wraps CON-/TRADICTORIOS, OB-/TENER, and EXPLO-/SIÓN; restores ESTE ES SU NÚMERO and DE where OCR omitted them; preserves the logical formula P∧¬P as one excluded unit; and corrects missing written accents in RAZÓN, EMPECÉ, TELÉFONO, ASÍ, CÓMO, SÍ, MAMÁ, and CARTÓN. OCR's OJ and standalone dash are drawing and speech-tail strokes, not printed textual units.

regions.labelEs: SI ASUMES AXIOMAS CONTRADICTORIOS, PUEDES OBTENER CUALQUIER COSA. SE LLAMA PRINCIPIO DE EXPLOSIÓN.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the possible condition, and asumes uses the ordinary present form for one familiar listener.
Axiomas is masculine despite its final -a, so contradictorios uses the matching masculine plural ending.
Contradictorios follows axiomas in the common neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Contradictorios uses masculine plural -os to match the masculine plural noun axiomas.
Puedes changes for one familiar listener, while obtener remains in its unchanged -er dictionary form as the possible action.
Cualquier appears before the singular noun cosa and keeps the shortened form used directly before a noun.
Se matches the one principle being named, llama is the corresponding form of llamarse, and principio de explosión fills the name slot.
Cualquier appears before singular cosa and keeps the shortened form used directly before a noun.
The two-word conversational expression marks the speaker's pause to test or consider the claim.

regions.labelEs: ¡OYE, TIENES RAZÓN! EMPECÉ CON P∧¬P Y HE CONSEGUIDO EL TELÉFONO DE TU MADRE!

excludedUnits.rationale: P∧¬P is symbolic propositional-logic notation for a proposition and its negation, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the affirmative tú command of oír and works as an attention-getter for one familiar listener.
Tienes matches one familiar listener, and razón completes the conventional expression for saying that person is right.
Empecé uses the completed-past form because it presents the start as one bounded event.
He is the speaker's present helper form of haber, and conseguido supplies the completed action whose result matters now.

excludedUnits.rationale: Lenhart is an unchanged personal surname, not a Spanish lexical word target.

applications.explanationEn: The conventional two-word expression briefly interrupts the exchange while the speaker checks something.
Es is a form of ser because su número identifies what the masculine demonstrative este refers to rather than locating it.
Cómo keeps its written accent because it begins a direct question, even though the speaker trails off.

regions.labelEs: HOLA, SOY UN AMIGO DE... SÍ, ¡ESTOY LIBRE ESTA NOCHE!

applications.explanationEn: Soy is a form of ser because un amigo states the speaker's claimed identity rather than a location.
Estoy matches the speaker, and libre describes the speaker's current availability.
Esta uses its feminine singular form to match noche in the standard two-word time expression.

regions.labelEs: ¡NO, EL VINO DE CARTÓN SUENA GENIAL!

applications.explanationEn: Vino names the drink, and de cartón identifies its carton or box packaging.
Suena is followed directly by genial, which supplies the speaker's description of how the idea sounds.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.

cards.answerEn: you assume; you accept as a starting point
cards.noteEn: Asumes is the present form of asumir used with one familiar listener. In reasoning, asumir can mean accepting an idea temporarily as a premise.

example.es: Asumes que el dato es correcto.
example.en: You assume that the fact is correct.

cards.noteEn: An axioma is a statement accepted as a starting point in a system of mathematics or logic. Axiomas is its plural form.

example.es: La demostración parte de dos axiomas.
example.en: The proof starts from two axioms.

cards.promptEs: el/un problema y otros sustantivos masculinos en -ma
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish say un problema even though problema ends in -a?
cards.answerEn: Problema is masculine, so use el or un and masculine describing words with it.
cards.noteEn: A noun's ending is only a clue to its gender, not an absolute rule. Several common words of Greek origin ending in -ma are masculine, including el problema, el sistema, el tema, and el programa. Learn each noun together with its article because not every word ending in -ma follows this pattern.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: In classical logic, accepting both a claim and its negation makes it possible to derive any claim.
cards.noteEn: P∧¬P represents a proposition P together with ‘not P,’ a direct contradiction. The principle is called explosion because unrestricted conclusions then follow. The joke treats those conclusions as a way to obtain unrelated personal facts and plans rather than merely proving propositions.
Contradictorios describes masculine plural things whose claims cannot all be true together. Its -os ending matches a masculine plural noun.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Obtener follows the same stem change as tener in some forms: obtengo, obtienes, and so on.

example.en: I need to get a copy.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “any” before one singular thing?
cards.answerEn: Put cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier libro, cualquier opción.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as libro or opción. Before a noun, cualquiera shortens to cualquier. The noun stays singular even when the meaning is any one out of many. The plus sign in the Spanish prompt means “followed by.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks llamarse, “to be called”
cards.noteEn: Llamarse uses a matching small word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, and so on. With he, she, formal you, or one named thing, use se.

cards.questionEn: How do you state what a person or thing is called?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and a form of llamar, then give the name: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, and so on.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is llamarse. The small pronoun changes with the person: me llamo means “I am called,” te llamas is informal “you are called,” and se llama is used for he, she, formal you, or one named thing.
With se, llama is a form of llamarse used to state a person's or thing's name. Without se, llama can instead mean “calls.”
In logic or another technical field, principio can name a basic rule or proposition. This differs from al principio, which refers to the beginning of something.

example.es: Es un principio básico de la lógica.
example.en: It is a basic principle of logic.

cards.noteEn: In this named logical principle, explosión refers to the result that any claim can be derived after a contradiction is accepted. In that technical sense it does not describe a physical blast.

example.es: La explosión es un resultado de la lógica clásica.
example.en: Explosion is a result in classical logic.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a ver, “let's see”
cards.noteEn: In the conversational expression a ver, a combines with ver rather than expressing movement toward a place.

example.en: Let's see, show me the map.

cards.questionEn: How can you pause to inspect or consider something with the sense of “let's see” or “let me see”?
cards.answerEn: Use the short expression a ver.
cards.noteEn: A ver often introduces a pause while the speaker checks, considers, or waits to discover something. The two words work together as a conversational expression; it is not the same as haber, the one-word verb used in forms such as hay.

example.en: Let's see, what do we have here?

cards.noteEn: Ver normally means to see. After a in the short expression a ver, it helps signal that the speaker is pausing to inspect, consider, or find something out.
Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is right?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of tener followed by razón.
cards.noteEn: Spanish describes someone as “having reason” rather than using ser with a word for “right.” Tener changes for the person and time: tengo razón means “I am right,” and tienes razón means “you are right.” Razón stays unchanged.
Empecé is the completed-past form of empezar used for yo. The spelling changes from z to c before é so the consonant sound stays the same.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Conseguido is the completed-action form of conseguir. After he, it says that the speaker has succeeded in obtaining a stated thing.
Teléfono can name the device itself or the number used to call someone. Context distinguishes the two senses.

example.es: Apunté tu teléfono en mi agenda.
example.en: I wrote your phone number in my address book.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

cards.questionEn: What does ¡Un momento! mean when someone interrupts or suddenly realizes something?
cards.answerEn: It means “Wait a moment!” or “Hold on!”
cards.noteEn: This fixed conversational interruption can ask someone to pause, or it can announce that the speaker has just noticed something important. Its function is broader than literally measuring one moment.

example.es: ¡Un momento! Creo que tengo la llave.
example.en: Hold on! I think I have the key.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.answerEn: your (formal or plural, before one thing)
Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Amigo can identify a male friend or appear as the masculine dictionary form when discussing the word itself.

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is available or not busy at a particular time?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar followed by libre.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time: estoy libre, está libre, and so on. Libre stays the same for one man or woman and becomes libres for more than one person. Ser libre usually describes being free rather than availability in a schedule.
With estar, libre can describe a person who has no commitment at a particular time. Libre has the same singular form for masculine and feminine people.

cards.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for “tonight”?
cards.noteEn: Esta means “this” and uses its feminine singular form to match noche. Spanish normally uses this two-word time expression without a preposition.

example.en: We are having dinner together tonight.

cards.noteEn: Vino is the masculine noun for wine. The same written form can also be a past form of venir, but a drink or packaging context identifies the noun.

cards.questionEn: What common Spanish expression refers to wine sold in a carton or box?
cards.answerEn: Say vino de cartón for boxed or carton wine.
cards.noteEn: Vino names the drink, while de cartón identifies the type of packaging. The expression often suggests inexpensive wine, especially in Spain.

example.es: Compraron vino de cartón para la fiesta.
example.en: They bought boxed wine for the party.

cards.answerEn: in; packaged as (linking a product to its container)
cards.noteEn: De can link a product to a noun that identifies its packaging. It does not say that the product itself is made from that packaging material.

example.es: La tienda vende cerveza de lata.

cards.noteEn: Cartón names cardboard and can also refer to packaging made from it, such as a carton or box.

example.es: Guardó la leche en un cartón.
example.en: She kept the milk in a carton.

cards.noteEn: Suena is the form of sonar used for one thing that gives an impression. A describing word can follow it directly; sonar a is a different pattern used before a noun or comparison.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something sounds or seems a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of sonar followed directly by a describing word.
cards.noteEn: Sonar changes to match the thing giving the impression: la idea suena, las ideas suenan. The describing word also changes when needed to match that thing: razonable becomes razonables. Do not add a before a describing word; sonar a is the separate pattern used before a noun or comparison, as in suena a excusa.
